title: Europe's Heatwave Becomes an Energy Crisis as France Shuts Nuclear Reactors and Rhine Shipping Stalls
excerpt: Record temperatures have forced France to cut 6.4 GW of nuclear power while the Rhine River drops to its lowest mid-July level in decades, compounding Europe's energy woes from the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
body:
• France has shut down three nuclear reactors and reduced output at eight more as river temperatures rise too high for safe cooling, cutting 6.4 GW of nuclear generation — about 14% of the country's total power demand.
  • The Rhine River has dropped to its lowest mid-July level in decades, hiking diesel shipping costs from Rotterdam to southern Germany by more than 50% in a single week.
  • A gas-fired power plant in southern France has also gone offline for the first time since 2022, adding further strain to a grid already squeezed by nuclear outages.
  • The energy disruption compounds the inflationary pressure from the ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis, with Brent crude topping $90 a barrel for the first time since June.

Europe's brutal early summer heatwave has crossed the threshold from public health emergency to energy crisis. Across France and Germany — the continent's two largest economies — record-breaking temperatures are shutting down power plants, drying up critical shipping routes, and driving up costs for consumers and industry at a moment when the global energy system can least afford it.

France's Nuclear Fleet Under Siege

France, which depends on nuclear energy for roughly 70% of its electricity, has been forced to slash generation by 6.4 gigawatts this week alone — equivalent to about 14% of the country's total daily power demand. The state energy company EDF shut down reactors at the Golfech plant on the Garonne River, Bugey on the Rhône, and Chooz on the Meuse, while eight additional reactors are running at reduced power, according to Reuters.

"We have seen two waves of climate-related unavailabilities that were unprecedented in both severity and timing, involving reactors that are not normally affected."

— Thibault Laconde, founder of climate analytics firm Callendar

The problem is straightforward physics: nuclear plants require vast quantities of river or sea water for cooling, and French regulators cap the temperature of water that can be returned to waterways. When rivers get too warm, reactors must throttle back or shut down entirely. An additional 2.5 GW of capacity is offline at the Chooz plant due to low water levels on the Meuse, which is subject to a water-sharing agreement with Belgium.

For the first time this summer, a gas-fired plant has also been knocked out. EDF took the 930-megawatt Martigues facility offline after Mediterranean Sea temperatures climbed too high for cooling — the first such outage since 2022.

The Rhine Runs Dry — Again

In Germany, the 800-mile Rhine River — Europe's most important inland shipping corridor — has dropped to its lowest mid-July level in decades. At the Kaub chokepoint between Koblenz and Mainz, water is so shallow that barges cannot carry full loads, according to Bloomberg data.

The result is immediate and expensive. Freight costs to ship diesel from Rotterdam to southern Germany have spiked more than 50% in the past week. The Rhine carries an enormous volume of coal, diesel, and industrial goods for Germany, France, Switzerland, and the Netherlands, and any disruption cascades across the continent's supply chains.

Germany has been here before. In 2018, critically low Rhine levels caused a 1.5% decline in industrial production and shaved 0.4% off GDP, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. The end-June heatwave alone cost the German economy an estimated €6 billion ($6.8 billion), according to an analysis by economic research firm Prognos for Handelsblatt.

A Double Energy Shock

The timing could not be worse. Europe is already paying sharply higher energy prices because of the Strait of Hormuz crisis, where US-Iran hostilities have disrupted oil and gas shipments. Brent crude topped $90 a barrel on Monday — its highest since June 11 — after rising nearly 16% last week.

The heatwave adds a second supply shock on top of the first. With nuclear generation curtailed, shipping corridors constrained, and electricity demand surging as millions of Europeans run fans and air conditioning, grid operators are scrambling. Britain narrowly avoided blackouts on June 23 when actual power demand hit 35 GW — far above the 29.7 GW peak that the National Energy System Operator had forecast.

What It Means for India and the Diaspora

For India, the energy crunch in Europe adds another layer to an already difficult global picture. Higher European energy costs feed into global commodity prices that India, which imports roughly 85% of its crude oil, cannot escape. The RBI flagged the Middle East war and erratic monsoon as risks to India's growth outlook just days ago.

NRIs living in Europe face a more immediate impact. Energy bills across France, Germany, and the UK have already risen due to the Hormuz-linked oil price surge, and the heatwave-driven grid stress could push prices higher through the summer. Climate scientists warn that three or four such intense heatwaves per summer may become the norm for Western Europe, suggesting this is not a one-off disruption but a structural shift in the continent's energy calculus.
